A few words to know

category
A group of similar items.
editorial enquiry
A question sent to newspaper staff.
inconclusive
Not enough to prove an answer.
retrieve
To find and get a stored item.
correspondent
A person who sends letters.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The archivist's response arrived with a copy of the newspaper's 2011 filing guide. It was not the missing correspondence Emma had hoped to inspect, but it corrected an assumption she had almost allowed into her reporting.

The newspaper had kept readers' letters, editorial enquiries and material supplied for information in separate index sections. The three October entries about the Glenarraidh Education Trust's student travel programme came from different categories. The headings were created by staff to help them retrieve documents; they were not reliable quotations from their authors.

“So they're three different people?” Sarah asked when Emma rang.

“There's no reason to assume that. The categories describe how the newspaper handled the material, not who sent it. One person might have contacted the paper several times.”

The entry dated 12 October 2011, bearing the phrase “decision not received”, appeared in the information section. That placement was interesting but inconclusive. It did not establish that the author had been an applicant, that a notice had failed to arrive or that a review deadline had been missed. Even the description might reflect an editor's interpretation rather than the original wording.

Emma recorded the section names and the archivist's explanation alongside the dates. Access to the letters themselves remained restricted while the archive considered privacy requirements.

Later Fiona Bell sent an inventory of boxes held by the foundation. It listed the outgoing correspondence ledger, some office guidance and the folder headed “Appeals and reviews — Student Travel 2011”. The document was an inventory, not an examination of the contents. Fiona repeated that the appeals folder had not been opened and no complete set of completed decision notices had been verified.

Emma asked whether the inventory showed that students had been told about the fourteen-day review procedure.

“No,” Fiona replied. “It tells us what was filed, not what was communicated.”

The answer brought Emma back to a distinction that had become central to her investigation. The newspaper recorded what its staff had received and classified. The trust recorded—or had intended to record—what its staff prepared and sent. Neither institution's surviving summary could establish what any particular student had understood.

Sarah sounded frustrated. “We keep getting descriptions of documents instead of the documents.”

“Descriptions are useful when we know their limits,” Emma said. “They're dangerous when we forget them.”

She drafted two precise requests. To the archivist she asked for a non-identifying description of the October item, if the rules allowed it. To Fiona she asked whether any general guidance explained when decision notices should reach applicants. She sought procedures, not private names.

Before pressing send, Emma glanced at her notes from the 18 September 2011 interview. Claire had warned her about asking the wrong questions. Emma could not know exactly what Claire had intended by those words. But she finally understood what a wrong question could do: it could force uncertain evidence to produce an answer it had never contained.

She sent both requests, leaving the identity of the writer—and the contents of the appeals folder—unresolved.
